newsitem.title: ROMANIA: FEATURE - Unsophisticated, cheap Dacia Romania's favourite.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Unsophisticated, cheap Dacia Romania's favourite.

text.p: The unsophisticated Dacia car produced in Romania for nearly 30 years is still by far the most popular vehicle among consumers coping with post-communist economic hardship.
And with good reason.

"What other brand new car can you buy for less than $4,000?" asked a high school teacher queuing for more than five hours at one of six Dacia dealers in Pitesti -- site of the carmaker's headquarters 110 km (70 miles) north of Bucharest.
"We do our best to meet demand," said one dealer.
"It was only recently that we managed to supply cars without putting people on a waiting list."

Automobile Dacia SA, a product of executed dictator Nicolae Ceausescu's ambitions to turn Romania into an industrial power, put out cars under a Renault licence until the early 1980s. It has made and sold 1.9 million.

Times have changed since the Ceausescu era, when buying a Dacia -- a status symbol -- meant putting yourself on a five-year waiting list. Top-ranking Communist Party officials negotiated de luxe versions with special options or interiors.

Even today, cars do not last long in showrooms. With average salaries stuck at about $80 per month, luxury cars remain the preserve of an elite earning high salaries, and the Dacia remains the obvious target for most aspiring car owners.
"We rarely have cars in stock," said Dacia spokesman Nicolae Badiu. "We must meet local demand and export too."

Some 45 percent of Dacia's output since its creation in 1968 has been destined to cope with potholed roads in other ex-communist east European countries or further afield, like Asia and Latin America.
LOCAL MARKET A PRIORITY
But priority now is for the local market.
"This year we will export only about 25 percent of a forecast output of 100,000 cars," said Dacia general manager Constantin Stroe. "Local demand must first be met."
After holding a virtual monopoly on the car market under communism, Dacia teetered on the brink of collapse in the early 1990s with cheap imports flooding in after Ceausescu's demise.

"It was a time when Romanians wanted any car other than the Dacia," said Dan Vardie, president of the Romanian motoring journalists' association. "They brought in second-hand western cars, some retrieved from junk yards."
Buyers came back to Dacia because of quality improvements and, more importantly, attempts to keep prices low. The firm employs 28,000 people and a million others depend on it for supplying vehicles.

"Dacia's evolution contradicted all forecasts. After the collapse of communism it went through a backslide. Everyone thought it would die," Vardie said. "But it recovered quickly and in less than two years became Romania's largest exporter."

The box-like exterior of the Dacia, a variation of the Renault 12, has remained much the same over the years, but the firm has tried hard to diversy its output range. Last year saw the introduction of a new model, Dacia Nova, with a new body, a more powerful engine and better fuel consumption.
The Dacia plant posted a 52 billion lei ($7.3 million) profit last year, in contrast with most state-run businesses saddled with heavy debt and payment arrears too vast to keep up production.

"Romanians buy Dacia cars because they're relatively cheap and easy to maintain and spare parts are readily available," said Dumitru Chivu, a driver and mechanic, who also spent half the day queueing at a dealer's.
UNAFRAID OF FOREIGN COMPETITION
With such optimistic sales figures, Dacia seems unafraid of the prospect of competition -- mainly from South Korea's Daewoo, which moved into the market two years ago.
"Competition is good for business. Higher demands from the South Koreans help our own suppliers improve the quality of their products," Stroe said.

Seeking a foothold in Romania's market as an entry to East European outlets, Daewoo Heavy Industries Ltd struck a joint venture with a local car maker which once produced under licence the Citroen Visa-based Oltena.
Though its models cost more than twice the price of a simple Dacia, business was good for a time and Daewoo committed almost $1 billion in investment up to the turn of the century.

But the new centrist government's policy of liberalising prices pushed monthly inflation to 30 percent in March and demand fell off sharply. Daewoo laid off thousands of workers in April and suspended production for a week of its Cielo car -- which sells for up to $13,600.
Sales have picked up but monthly production stands at no more than 3,500 from a peak last December of more than 4,500.
"It's ultimately a matter of price and purchasing power," Vardie said. "You can buy three Dacias for the price of a Cielo."
Romanian consumers are, however, becoming more discerning, price permitting.
"Dacia ought to come up with better quality," said another buyer in the Pitesti queue. "It's easy to maintain but breaks down frequently. It's turned most drivers into mechanics."
Eyeing west European markets, where consumers demand environmentally-clean cars, as well as China, Turkey, Egypt and Algeria, Dacia plans to overhaul its longstanding model.
"We will equip our cars with a non-polluting engine this year," Stroe said.
Long-term plans are for a car befitting the 21st century.
"We've started manufacturing a car for the year 2000 in cooperation with prestigious companies from abroad," Stro said, without elaborating.
Last year, the plant had extensive talks with France's Peugeot PEUP. PA about assembling the Peugeot 306 in Romania. Industry ministry sources talked at the time of a possible joint venture.
"We have to link up with several Western producers for manufacturing car parts," Stroe said. "I'm optimistic we can do this given our experience and skilled labour force." ($ = 7080 Romanian Lei)
